utterances.text: From what we knew, three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see about Kole that led you to the conclusion that he was a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: For the most part, that is people who knew him better - I only knew him by sight - the people who knew him were saying that he was considerably better than the other shift commanders, and probably when his shift was on that we would fare better. But as far as my personal encounters with Kole, he asked us to move a truck, and we pushed the truck to the area around Rooms 3 and 4. But people who were on the shift addressed him, and by the way they did so, we thought that he was a shift commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe the individual for us?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I could describe him. Dark, could be about 175 centimetres tall, dark, tanned complexion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see him often in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently. That is, throughout my stay in the camp, whenever his shift was on, we would see him for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that you would recognise this individual if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We know each other well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom today, please, and tell us if he is here, and if so, where he is?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is seated to the right between --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the full sentence, but perhaps I could ask you, sir, where are you looking? Would you point and tell us what row this individual is that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Kole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Between the first two police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you looking from right to left or from left to right, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He was to the right, next to the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to have to do this. If we are looking at the window you're looking at, there are six chairs starting from right to left. Could you count the number of chairs from the window from right to left and tell us which seat the person is occupying?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Chair number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, identifies Kole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said there were three shifts. Did you know any other shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the person we called Kajin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen on the day after your arrest that you recall?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the night when I was beaten, the following morning, because I was covered in blood and practically could not move my arm, I thought that I was losing a lot of blood and that I didn't stand a good chance of surviving. Some of the prisoners who were around me told me that the next morning, Kajin would come on duty and that he was a good guy and that I should try to talk to him, and that the next morning, probably some of the inmates would be sent to the hospital in order to be given medical care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you in fact address -- we are now going to 22. I'll come back to paragraph 20 in a minute. Did you in fact seek help from Kajin?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that. That is, the following morning, I think it could have been 9.00 or 10.00 in the morning, it doesn't matter. At any event, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Kajin was about 10 to 15 metres away from Room 1. He was wearing a military trousers with suspenders, and I said that I had heard that some people who were injured would be taken to the hospital to have their injuries treated, and I showed him what had happened to me and I asked if I could be in that group. He asked me, "Who did this to you?" However, I simply shrugged and turned away. He said that he would put me in that group, and he made good on that promise. And unfortunately, in the van taking us to the hospital -- to the hospital that day, Zoran Zigic was also taking a ride.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to your being taken to hospital, sir, but you had dealings with Kajin. Did you know this person called Kajin before the conflict, before your stay at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think we all knew each other by sight. I think we knew each other from the technical school, the middle -- the secondary school. His brother was also a student there and I was one of the students.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you knew him from school days, and did you know his brother?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew his brother. He was the one who later took me to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We will get to that in a moment as well. Now, sir, at Keraterm, during the period of your stay from the 14th of June until early August, 1992, did you have -- did you have opportunities to see Kajin on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him every time when his shift was on. That is, throughout my stay there, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be able to recognise that individual if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom and tell us whether you see him today?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where he is seated, using the same sort of method as we did earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He is seated in chair number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear, you're still counting from right to left from the window towards you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For the record, identifies Kajin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have another conversation -- well, we will get to that in a little bit too. Do you know who the leader of the third shift was?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: In my mind, it was Sikirica, or Sikira as we called him. However, that was my view, but I did not think about it that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and how did you learn his name?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I learned his name in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the individual for us as you recall him at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think he was brown-haired, dark hair, about 165, 170 centimetres tall, and I don't think that he was clean shaven, and he had his hair a little bit, I don't know, unruly, we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you believe that you would recognise that individual as Sikirica or Sikira if you were to see him again?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look around the courtroom, please, and tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend hasn't laid the ground at all for how often this man has been seen, and I object unless he's going to do that properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you lay a foundation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I shall, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I was trying to move along but my friend is quite correct, and I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your stay at Keraterm, are you able to tell us how often you saw the individual you referred to as Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I saw him fairly frequently. That is, like the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you knew him before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under what circumstances and how frequently would you have been able to see him before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It was a slight acquaintance. It was like seeing people in town and you remember their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him at Keraterm, did you then recognise him as someone you had seen before the war? In other words, by the time you were at Keraterm, did you recognise him already?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I knew that face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you arrived at Keraterm, you were not able to put a name to the face; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned the name from other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name you learned from other prisoners, sir, do you recognise that face in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if he's here and, if so, where he is?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's in chair number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again for the record, that's from the window, counting right to left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For the record, please, identifies the accused Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, skipping ahead then, you told us that - and I want to go through this relatively quickly - after speaking to Kajin and getting permission to go to the hospital, is it true that you and six or seven other prisoners were taken to the hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you made reference earlier that, unfortunately, Zoran Zigic was one of your escorts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of another inmate who was injured who accompanied you and Zoran Zigic to the hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Among others was Emsud Bahonjic, Jasmin Colic, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And en route to the hospital, is there an incident involving Mr. Zigic and Emsud that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zigic beat Emsud throughout this time and mistreated him, but the driver who was driving the van tried to take away the weapon from him and to calm him down and prevent him from bothering us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once at the hospital, did you see anything in relation to Emsud Bahonjic that Mr. Zigic did?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: A physician was examining Emsud, and Zigic said that he was not to do anything there because he was a sniper. He was on a gurney, and he was brought back very quickly. Zigic approached him and put a cross on his forehead, and Emsud, who was half conscious, kept saying that he was not guilty of anything, that his children did nothing, but Zigic kept accusing him that -- of being a sniper and put that cross on his forehead, and I think that that's how he died too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, while at the hospital, did you overhear any conversation about Emsud requiring an X-ray?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were saying that he needed an X-ray because he probably had these serious internal injuries, but Zigic said that nothing was to be done with him because he had to take him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, do you know whether Emsud received an X-ray or treatment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. He was brought back to the camp and no medical help was given him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about you, did you receive any medical help?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I waited, that is, we were called in one by one. Nurse was there who happened to know my sister-in-law. They worked together. So she quickly asked me about her husband, asked me whether I knew anything, and she said that she would try to help as much as she could. All this was in passing. And she did what we could. She put on pieces of gauze on my head and then she gave me some netting which I pulled over my head. Then she also treated my head and gave me a bandage so that I could bandage my arm myself, and this was all she was able to do in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The doctor was there standing to the side. He was talking to the other people who were injured. I don't know how much help he provided them, but I know that we were all taken back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I phrased my question very badly. Were you personally treated by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your broken fingers set?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you came back to Keraterm after having been taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: All those who had been -- who had been brought there, that is, who were given a chance to get some treatment, were returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the same day or did you stay overnight?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That includes Emsud Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to Emsud in a minute, sir, I'm not finished. But very, very briefly, and I don't think my friends are going to object to this, is it true, sir, at Keraterm you -- the food rations consisted of two small slices of bread and a bowl of water with perhaps a leaf of cabbage in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection. Incorrect characterisation and leading. What is "small"? If he's going to lead, we do, but adjectives are for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be quicker if I have the witness do it rather than me try to lead it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you get for food, sir, at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: When we would receive food, and it happened that for a day or two we did not receive any, what they called a small piece -- a small loaf, that was one loaf sliced into very thin slices. It was a slice that I could have eaten in two or three mouthfuls, and I could have eaten it in no time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than bread, did you get anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: For the most part it was a leaf of cabbage with hot water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have unlimited time to eat?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. This was done in such a way that we would do it as fast as possible and run back to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen if you didn't do it as fast as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It depended on the shift. For the most part, guards would approach certain prisoners. They would ask money of them. They would beat them or they would put a knife against the stomach and ask where the money was, ask if the money was buried somewhere, or if they would beat prisoners, then there would be two or three beatings. So people really looked to eat as quickly as possible and go back to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that toilet facilities were very inadequate. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn now, if I may, to an incident that you recall when prisoners were being called out at night. Can you tell us about that and tell us whose shift was on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Inmates were called at night regardless of whose shift was on duty, but most frequently they were taken out during the shifts manned by the Banovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Do you recall an incident one night when Kole's shift was on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that occasion -- on that occasion, a large number of prisoners were called out, they were taken out, and then they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 beaten. We could hear moans and screams, and this took a long time. And I heard a voice, I think it was one of the Banovic brothers, he was saying, "Put a jacket over him so that he doesn't scream as much." After it was over, again I think it was Banovic, I think I recognised his voice, he said, "Where were you? You were too late for the beating."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies, the witness said that there was -- that there was the Banovic brothers, and Kondic was also mentioned as being in the shift, and it was not entered into the record. So if I can ask for that correction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The correction will be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, from your observation or any other source of information, led you to conclude that the night you're talking about was Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The shift change was usually done before the nightfall, and from what we knew, that is whose shift would come next, this is how we were able to identify whose shift was on when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the night that you're talking about, had the shift changed to Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were changing it around 6.00 or 7.00 in the evening, and I think that they had come on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You earlier told us, sir, about the frequency of these kinds of nightly beatings. How often would these things happen?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: This happened almost nightly. If it would not happen in Room 2, then it would happen in Room 1 or in another room, but it usually did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it matter whose shift was on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that in Kajin's shift, and to a degree Kole's shift, it was less frequent. We thought that when they were on, that we were somewhat safe, but if he weren't -- if he wasn't around, then we would fare the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us earlier about Emsud Bahonjic, and after you came back from the hospital, did anything further happen to Emsud Bahonjic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I know that Zigic asked that his sniper be brought out. Then he beat him again, and then half an hour later he ordered us to carry him back in. We did. And a couple of days later, he turned for worse. He was breathing heavily. We asked to bring him out to fresh air. We got the permission, but Zigic reappeared a while later, started yelling, and we had to bring him back in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us earlier that Zigic had accused Emsud of being a sniper coming back from the hospital. Is that to whom he was referring when he said, "Bring out my sniper"? Or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He was referring exclusively to Emsud. Emsud told me that when he came to the Keraterm camp the first time around, that Zigic had approached him, tapped him on the shoulder and said, "You are a sniper. You were killing people," and it was from there on that it all started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, I have to again comment on the report. He said that the witness said that during Kole's shift and Kajin's shift it was more often, and he then said that when they would leave, that he was not -- that this would not happen, so it was not clear in the sense in which the witness had said it, so I would like it to be fully clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I can ask a couple more questions to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Backing up if we can just for a moment, please, sir, to your knowledge, did beatings happen on all three shifts?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly to say that on Kajin's shift, and sometimes Kole's shift, those beatings would be less frequent?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were less frequent. What is probably in dispute is that, for instance, if there was Kajin's shift, if he was physically present there and had control over it, then there wasn't as much beating and mistreatment. However, if he was -- his shift was on and he was not present, it would start immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, just to finish up about Emsud Bahonjic, before we were interrupted, are you aware that Mr. Bahonjic ultimately died?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within two or three days of coming out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Somewhere around there, two, three, four days. In any event, he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before he died, did he tell you anything that Zigic had said to him about being a sniper?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told him that Zigic, at the very entrance to the camp, had approached him and told him that he had been a sniper and he was killing innocent Serbian people, and from that day on, Zigic started beating him. Frequently Duca also took part in these beatings. And that was the reason why he was being beaten all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever admit to being a sniper in your presence?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your stay at Keraterm, you've made reference in earlier testimony to Banovic. Did you know anyone by the name of Banovic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew two brothers, twins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they look alike?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any way to distinguish between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: One could tell them apart because one of them -- and we told them apart because one of them, I think, was better, much better than the other one, whom we called Cupo. First, in terms of his sections [phoen], Cupo, we called because he had long hair, hair down to his shoulders. Whenever he was in the camp, or did rounds of the camp, he often carried a baseball bat in his hands, and that is how we could tell them apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the word "Cupo" mean something in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It means a man with a lot of hair, with long hair, somebody who has long hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the nickname Cupo was referred to by his description, then?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was his nickname. That's how we called him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn your mind to an incident about the 1st of July, 1992, in the late evening hours. Do you remember whether Cupo did something to you or to your inmate companions?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of July, in the evening of the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm referring to, sir. Or approximately that date.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That day, that day, was the first time that we were given slightly better food. I think it was beans that we had for lunch, even though it happened at dusk. So we were coming out to get this food. However, the food distributed in a disastrous way. That is Kondic, Cupo, and others came up and began to beat and ill-treat the inmates. Kondic was the one who beat me most of all of them or -- I almost fainted when he hit me. Cupo and others were helping them in that, so I carried this bowl with food and it all spilled, and he beat me again and forced me to pick it all up, to wash up the vessel, and return it. And I somehow managed to get back into a dormitory and there I passed out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring now specifically to something that happened with Cupo Banovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, does he know whose shift that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whose shift was on in relation to the previous incident you told us about, about when the beans were being distributed and Kondic and I can't remember who else you said was there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, but I know that Kondic, Banovic, Sahadzija were on that shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "That shift." Were you able to assign that shift to a particular shift leader or are you not able to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think what he's saying is that he -- the witness says that he knows that Kondic, Banovic were on that shift. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift that shift was?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. All I do know is who beat me, and it was Kondic, Banovic. So that means they were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you've already made reference to an incident where you heard Cupo say something about taking a prisoner's jacket and putting it in his mouth. Do you remember any more details about that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened one night when they had taken inmates out to beat them. And Cupo was saying -- what I overheard was, "Put a jacket over his mouth so that he stops hollering."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know a couple of policemen, one by the name of Fikret and one by the name of Drago?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Indeed. They were brought to the camp. They arrived in police uniforms with army boots. They came to dormitory 2, and they told us that they had signed a document of loyalty to the Republika Srpska, and after the takeover of power, they had been working throughout since the takeover of power, but that that day, they demoted them or, rather, confiscated their weapon, their licence, and everything else that the police are issued with and were brought to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I may have asked you, but do you recall what date it was that they came to the camp or are you unable to give us a date?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: They were taken out during the night. Drago did not come back; Fikret did. And after that, I think he was taken to a hospital or something, but what Fikret told us is that they beat them with some iron chains, baseball bats, metal rods and things, and he said that Drago had succumbed, that he was killed. He somehow managed to get back alive, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father ended up becoming an inmate at Keraterm as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: My father was brought together with a group of men who had been rounded up in a village, Duracci, that is, he was hiding there with my mother and my wife, because my mother comes from that village. That is where she was born, and I believe it was the last Muslim village bordering on Donji Orlovci which had not been ethnically cleansed, but when the turn of that last village came up, he was rounded up with a number of other villagers. A number of those villagers were either killed or something. They are missing to this day. At any rate, I mean that they were taken aside, to a side and fire -- gunfire was heard and they're missing. But be that as it may, my father was not in that group. He was brought to Keraterm, and the next morning I found him in Room 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what shape was he in when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He had been badly beaten. His nose was broken. He had difficulty breathing. He told me that there was a Serb soldier who beat him particularly badly as he went off the bus, that is, one was beating him on the back, forcing him to get off the bus, and the other one met him outside. Why? Because that soldier was saying that in 1945 he had killed his father Radovan on Kozara, even though in 1945 my father was only 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time your father came to the camp, is my math correct, sir, he was 62?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was born in 1930 so that he was 62.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father stay in the camp very long?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He stayed in for about a fortnight. Then all those over 60 were called out, and from what we were told was that they would be transferred to the camp at Trnopolje. Fortunately, it did happen. Indeed, they were taking over there and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your father arrived in early July; is that correct? 1st or 2nd of July, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father ever interrogated, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. As he was over 60, men of that age were not -- at least they were not normally interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date. I think it was around the 5th or the 6th of July, beginning of July at any rate. And Kajin's brother came to take me for interrogation. He brought me into a room, and he just stayed behind, standing by the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've made reference to Kajin's brother earlier in your testimony in that you knew him before the war. Did you see him at Keraterm on occasions other than the day that he took you for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you see him at the camp and what position, if any, did he hold?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think he held any position in the camp. I usually saw him whenever he was on duty. I mean when his shift was on duty. I can't say what went on at night-time, but I do not think that this lad ever harmed anyone. At least of us, the witnesses, whenever we communicated what we could find out was -- what we learned from talking was that nobody was harmed by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I phrased it badly, sir, but you say "whenever he was on duty." When he was on duty, what did he do or what did he appear to be doing?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. I think he was just a guard. Perhaps he was -- that day perhaps he was one the guards. He called me out, escorted me to the interrogation room, and took me back to the dormitory. Whether he had any special duty, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift he was on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you to now turn your mind to the 20th of July, early afternoon, an incident where you were standing in line to get your lunch. Something happened that day, and tell us what you can recall and whose shift was on.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That day, lunch was distributed, that is, lunch as far as we could see. It seemed much better than before that, that is, more beans were poured into those bowls, but after that they began to torture and beat prisoners, and I've already pointed it out. I was mostly beaten by Kondic and by Cupo Banovic. Prisoners simply had no time, were given no chance to consume that food. It simply fell out of my hands, and they again beat me, forcing me to pick it all up and put it back into the bowl, wash it, and go back to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The witness has testified about it, the whole thing. That was couple of questions and a couple of answers. I think the whole line of questioning is a repetition here, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I hadn't referred the witness to the 20th of July, before. I referred him to -- I think the 1st of July I referred to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the 1st of July. This is new material. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift was on on the 20th of July, sir, the incident that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was Kole's shift. In any event, the guards were Sahadzija, Banovics, Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those guards, did you associate them with any particular shift?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we associated guards with the shift leaders. That is, we more or less knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, the witness mentioned Sahadjia, and his name does not figure in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That correction should be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you didn't finish your answer. Maybe you did. I asked you those guards what you referred to, did you associate them in any particular shift, and you said, "We associated guards with the shift leaders," and then we were interrupted. Do you remember what shift leaders you associated those particular guards with?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We usually -- I think that these guards were on Kole's shift. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Sahadzija that you mentioned earlier, sir, did you see him doing something while they was going on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew him in the camp because he seized watches from all inmates who had watches. He approached an inmate and demanded from him. He took out the knife, began to prick him in the stomach, asking for money or something. And that is what we called him, Sahadzija, watch man, because he always looked for inmates' watches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, we are approaching ten minutes to 4.00, when we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And I hope to finish this witness in the not-too-distant future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Arifagic, we will now take a break until ten minutes after 4.00. During the break, you're reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I'd like you to turn to an event, if you would, please, when -- I understand on the 21st of July, 1992, or thereabouts, you're aware that new buses of prisoners came to Keraterm and were placed in Room 3; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. The previous day, I think we were ordered to make room in Room 2. The people who were in Room 3 until then were then transferred. Part of them were transferred to Room 2 to -- one part to Room 1, one part to Room 4, and that Room 3 was cleared up, cleared for the arrival of people who were brought in that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And eventually, after Room 3 was cleared out in the way you've described, buses of new people arrived and they were placed in Room 3; is that fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, were these people coming in buses only or were there any that came in by truck?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were brought in by buses but a small part was also brought in by truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say anything about the use of that truck in regard to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It would happen sometimes that the prisoners were brought in directly by truck and they would be registered or something and then they would be loaded up back in on the truck. They would have to lie down. Up on the truck was a man with a rifle, and they would be taken back. Sometimes these trucks would come back at nightfall. We would then be asked to wash it because there was blood on it. And the next day the whole thing would be repeated again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the people that arrived in Keraterm and were placed in Room 3? Were they allowed to mingle with the balance of the Keraterm inmate population?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that the contact was established on the first day, that is when they were first put in Room 3. After that they would not be allowed to mingle with us, and we were also ordered to stay in our own rooms and not to have any contact with Room 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of the people who were placed in Room 3 after it had been emptied out?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some. The majority of these people were from some -- from an area near Prijedor that we called Brdo, from the villages around there, and I knew a person called Dzevad Ejupovic, who worked on the same construction with me. Jasim Causevic and Enver Causevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you told by them, or some of them, how many people were placed into Room 3?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: They told me that the room was very small, that it was overcrowded, that they did not have standing room, let alone sitting room, that there were 350 or 400 in there, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware that sometime on one occasion, an incident happened that's referred to as the Room 3 massacre. You're aware of that, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn your mind to the afternoon leading up to that evening and tell us what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: What I recall is that we had been ordered to go to our rooms and to stay locked in, and we were told that we could not go out. At dusk when the night had fallen, some strange sound could be heard. We could feel some vehicles moving, some voices and noises, and there was some commotion around the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: After that, I think it was about 10.00 or 11.00 at night, again some trucks started and people started arriving in the camp and we were completely locked up from outside. We heard an order telling us to lie down, not to raise our heads, not to move. From the direction of Room number 3 one could hear bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift was on duty that night?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Kole's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The shift was changed around 7.00 p.m., so we knew that it was his shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you see any particular guards on duty that night that you associated with Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw a guard, and I think that I had also seen him when the shift was changing and we were ordered -- when we had received that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to ask you to be specific. When you say "him," to whom are you referring, you had seen "him"?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I am referring to Kole. I saw him entering the camp when his shift was coming on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier in evidence hearing shooting. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The fire lasted 15, 20 minutes, maybe half an hour. And after that, it quieted down, but what I do -- what I remember, though, while we were lying down, the silence was resounding in our room because, from the -- from Room 3, we could hear moans and screams, and what I remember was a voice, somebody saying, "Don't touch Rooms 1 and 2." After that, there was quiet, but then the fire again started in about an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection to the translation. The witness has said in Bosnian, "Ne dirajte mi sobe 1 i 2," and it doesn't reflect exactly what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, do you recall what was said by this voice that you overheard?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: From what I heard, this voice was saying, "Don't even attempt to touch the Rooms 1 and 2," to me, and I think that he was referring to -- when he was saying "touch," don't shoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose voice that was?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert that. I think that it was Kole's, but I cannot assert that because I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the second round of shooting last?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that it also lasted about 15 to 20 minutes, up to half an hour, and at that point it was difficult to ascertain the time, how long it all lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any other conversation or did you hear any other questions being asked by anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear that, because the position in which I was in in Room 2, I was a bit farther away from the door, and what I could hear, though, was quite clear. It was not to touch Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. I'm taking you to a different point. After that I understand that there is a second burst of gunfire, and could you tell, sir, whether anyone else asked any other questions after the second burst of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. After that everything was quiet. We stayed in the rooms throughout the night and nothing else happened that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The following morning, sir, did you find out what had occurred during the shooting incidents you overheard? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The following morning what came to us was a word that many men in Room 3 had been killed, but we were not allowed to go out. I think that the room leader came and asked for volunteers, but we were afraid that the volunteers were being asked to probably go out and load up the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone from your room did volunteer?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that they did, but I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see happening?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: During that day a large truck appeared and the men who went out to load up the dead bodies. What I could see when the truck was leaving the perimeter, it was covered with a canopy and it was leaving a trail of blood. Then a fire vehicle arrived, that is, vehicles that we used for firefighting in Prijedor, and I think that the same men who had loaded up the bodies were also washing down the asphalt area in front of Room 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later speak to a Jasim Causevic who told you what he did?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to him. He was my brother-in-law's brother, and he was one of those who had volunteered and who had loaded up the dead bodies. What he told me was that about 99 to 100 men had been killed, that he had loaded them up in this trailer truck, that they were stacking them up four bodies high, and that the bodies were taken out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you know a Simo Drljaca before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That name was well known in Prijedor. He was a functionary with the SUP, and I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear, the SUP, that's S-U-P, is that the initials for some organisation?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's an acronym for the Secretariat of the Interior or the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the SUP were in charge of the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what Mr. Drljaca's position was -- I'm sorry, you may have said that. Do you know what his position was in relation to the SUP? If I'm asking you to repeat yourself, I apologise. I just didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that after the takeover of the power of the SDS in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca was the commander of SUP or the commander of the police station in Prijedor, as we used to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp after the incident that I'm going to refer to as the massacre?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about this and whether he was alone and how you saw him and when.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He arrived at the camp after the massacre. He was wearing a blue camouflage uniform, and it was wartime police uniform. He was escorted by certain men whom I did not know, but I did know him. What we were told was that this would not repeat itself, that this had been a mistake, and that we would be better protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in the presence of any other dignitaries?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that accompanying him was Sikirica, but I cannot assert that. I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it just the two of them, the person you think may have been Sikirica and Drljaca, or were there yet other people with them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. There were other persons wearing military uniforms but whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, just so that I'm clear, you said it was after the massacre. Was it the day following the massacre, like immediately after the massacre?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. After the first massacre, the next day there was another massacre in the camp. I think that about 40 people were killed on that occasion, and after the second massacre, Simo Drljaca came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, you've told us about your conversation with Jasim Causevic. Was there a point in time when you were able to get out and look at Room 3?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a day or two after the second massacre. The next day after the massacre, the washing took place again and all the rest, and then we had an opportunity to come out and communicate with Room 3. I went to the lavatory, and after that I just took a peep in Room 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to look around the grounds? Did you see any additional machine-gun placements that had not been there before?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the very machine-gun nest that I already mentioned that I saw being placed before that massacre, it was that machine-gun nest which was opposite Room 3, across the path. There was a table with a machine-gun 84, as we call it, and to the right of this machine-gun nest, facing Room 3, there was a searchlight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that additional machine-gun nest and a searchlight placed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection to this question because the witness has testified already that he had seen them after the massacre, in the morning, and now he has testified about the second time, and the Prosecutor is going third time about it when witness said that he has been out of the room the following day. So it's asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the question is permissible. Just confine your question to the additional machine-gun nest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand my question, sir? When did you first notice the searchlight and that machine-gun placement?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: When we first had the opportunity to come out after the massacre, it was there then. Before the massacre in Room 3, that machine-gun and that searchlight were not there because it was not one of the permanent sentry posts or machine-gun nests, as we called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. You've told us there was a second massacre the following day, and can you briefly tell us what you can recall about that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the same thing repeated about 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening. The gunfire could be heard for about 15 or 20 minutes, and what I could hear was a voice saying, "What are we going to do? There are still some who are alive." And then one could hear individual shots. I do not know why I started counting them, and I counted 43 shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, the morning after what we would call the second massacre, I understand that bodies were taken away. Did you see anyone present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, once again, those men who were called out loaded those bodies and then I think a truck, Zastava 640, a smallish truck, arrived, and what I could see, men who were loading those bodies were also put in that truck at the time we were leaving the camp. Before that, they were called out. And those who were considered sick or injured, they were also loaded on to that truck because they were told, "We are taking you for treatment."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who was present during the loading of that second truck on the second day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. We could not see it then, because we were not allowed to leave the rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that one of the people who had loaded the bodies the first night was someone you had spoken to by the name of Yasmin Causevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he one of the ones who was also involved in the loading of the bodies after the second shooting incident?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him again after the truck left with the second load of bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I saw him at that time when that truck was leaving, that is as it went past Room 2 and was heading for the gate. He was sitting to the right, I saw him sitting in that truck, and they moved towards the exit from the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen him since that date?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us earlier that -- no, let me rephrase that. Was there an incident, sir, that the person you identified as Kajin came to the inmates of your room and had a conversation with you about anything?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was after the first night of massacre, Kajin came to the front of our room and took the bars in -- and put his hands around the bars that had been made there. I think he had a pistol in his hand and was hitting the bars with it. And one could see from his voice that he was drunk. What he was saying, what he was explaining to us, was that he was the one who requested that Rooms 1 and 2 be let alone, that he was very sorry that all that had happened, that in the massacre he had lost very many of his friends, and what was happening to us at present, that we were paying for Kozara in 1941, that in principle he disagreed with the SDS policy, that he was for bringing to justice the man who was guilty and bringing whoever was guilty before a firing squad, but that he was definitely against people being tortured and beaten. Perhaps it sounds cynical, but I liked that at that moment, that there was somebody who perhaps believed that man who was found responsible should be judged and sentenced, but that people shouldn't be tortured and harmed, and I liked that. And when I talked to other inmates, I believe that many share this opinion, even though people still lost lives but nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Kajin's condition, from your estimation, at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I suppose in a very bad depression because I think that after that, one of the guards came and he called out to him -- or rather they told him to move away from the dormitory and go to the exit from -- through the gate to get out. I think he was feeling very bad but he knows best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us about Zoran Zigic, and did you know someone named Duca?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen during your stay at Keraterm involving Zigic and Duca? In specific I'm referring to an incident with brothers Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen. When I arrived in the camp, there were two brothers, Zijad and Ilijaz Jakupovic whom I knew really well. We were even related. I think it was on the first or the second day, I'm not sure, but Duca and Zigic came and requested that the two guys come out -- or rather they were looking for Jakupovics who had raped a Serb girl. So they brought them out and beat them right at the exit from Room 2. And to the right there was a truck, and since Duca was very strong, he was hitting Ilijaz against the truck requesting that he confess to that deed, and at some point Ilijaz said that he may kill him but he is not going to confess it because he had not done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you witnessed these people being beaten, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. One could see it because it was happening in front of Room 2 and when those men came inside, their faces -- I think they could not really see where they were. All one would see was just blue blotches. Their faces looked like pulp. You couldn't recognise eyes or nose or anything. Their faces were all swollen with blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. I understand, sir, there came a time in early August that you were actually transferred from Keraterm to Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I can just summarise, I understand that the guards told you that names would be called and you were going to be loaded on to buses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the explanation was the following. All those who are called out are to go out and board buses, and after that, buses will come to dormitories, first to dormitory 1, without any callout, inmates can get out, and when the dormitory 1 is empty, then it will move on to dormitory 2, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I understand that ultimately the prisoners got on buses and you were taken to Keraterm; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, what did I say? Keraterm? No, sorry. You were taken from Keraterm put on buses and taken to Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my fault. Once you got to Trnopolje, sir, did you see Zoran Zigic again?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived there, we were put in -- on a lawn, on a meadow in front of the cultural centre in Trnopolje, and to the right or to the left of us, depending on where you looked from, there was a wire Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 fence, and we were told that we were allowed to be in that area but that we were not to mix with other inmates, and so, since we had barely arrived, were looking at this grass, where to lie down, because the night was falling. And at that moment, Zoran Zigic came through the camp entrance and started looking for his kum, for his best man, and this one called back to him and began to beat him with his boots and with whatever. He beat him up badly. And then the -- whatever, either the shift leader or somebody, I don't know, who took Zigic out and promised us that that would never happen again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the same Zoran Zigic that was at Keraterm that came to Trnopolje and beat a prisoner, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand you stayed at Trnopolje until the 1st of October and before leaving the camp, you had to sign a document of some sort. What was that and tell us what that was for?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: As we were explained, all of us, the inmates who were to be registered by the International Red Cross, had to apply for emigration, and after we signed those applications, we were issued the dispositions of the then authorities in Prijedor, that pursuant to Article such and such that we were being authorised to emigrate, to move out of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign such a document?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did this document say?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That document said, "At the request of Jusuf Arifagic who applied to such-and-such on such-and-such a date for permission to leave the territory of the municipality Prijedor within so many days," something like that, and after that, we were issued that authorisation. We were registered, boarded buses, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mention made of your property and what would happen to it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody raised that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, shortly after you got to Trnopolje, I understand that a video crew came and took a video of the prisoners from Keraterm that had arrive at Trnopolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your stay at Keraterm, can you tell the Court what happened, if anything, to your body weight as a result of your stay there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think I lost about 27 or 8 kilogrammes. What I remember well is that when I arrived in Trnopolje, we, and I've already said that, we were ordered not to mix with other inmates in the Trnopolje camp, that supposedly they would be moved over to Keraterm to be interrogated, that we had already done our bit. And I was in such a state that I couldn't even pronounce some letters, S or Z and other. I know that this wire fence which was around, that people in Trnopolje had more food than we did. I remember that. And they tried to pass on some bread to us, or at times they would throw over that fence perhaps half a kilogramme or a loaf of bread, and there would be a huge throng, a huge crowd of men who went for that -- for that bread and would end up with a handful of dust because that would be it. Afterwards, when we came in touch with those people, they were explained that they were not to communicate with us because we were extremists and that we would be all liquidated, as likely as not, and that it was better for them to keep away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand that you have seen a copy of the video that was taken of you and your fellow inmates from Keraterm at Trnopolje, and you can see yourself on that video; is that correct? You've seen that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With the assistance of the AV, I'd like to play a 90-second clip at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you can tell us, sir, if you recognise the people from Keraterm there and where, if anywhere, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's only 90 seconds, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you've seen this before?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Could you back up a couple of frames, please, Mr. AV. Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see yourself in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take the pointer, please, and point out where you are in this clip?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on the video. Yes. Okay. I'm sorry. I guess we really can't point out on the video. Perhaps you could describe to the Court, from right to left, if you are visible, in fact, and where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in the upper right corner, in the upper right corner. I have a beard. In front of me in Fikret Avdic, another Keraterm inmate, and I am to the right, to the right in the upper right corner. All you can see is my head and hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be safe to say that you are the tallest individual visible from right to left almost immediately under the ICTY emblem?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate for Your Honours where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your body is not visible but your head is; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: There are two men behind me, behind, who are taller than the rest, and I'm the one to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just let the video quickly scan through, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court from looking here, please, whether or not you can tell how many of these people were from Keraterm before they came here. Do you know this individual that's shown now?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. All these men here are from Keraterm more or less. They could have -- because we were always separated from other Trnopolje inmates. So if there is somebody here from the Trnopolje camp, then it's perhaps 1 per cent or maybe 2 who come to bring us some food. All the others are the camp inmates who had been transferred there from Keraterm a day before this tape was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that video be marked in these proceedings, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think we're up to 22, if I'm not mistaken. 22? Thank you. Very briefly, I think I can finish this witness in the next five minutes. One last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to raise a matter. I've already expressed some concerns to my learned friend about the exercise that he's going to do, and I'd like to develop those a little bit. He's going to seek to deal with the witness with a large number of names listed in a book. There is information given in the book about the disappearance or death of the people listed in there. It is not obvious from the book what the provenance of that information is. The danger, in my submission, is that the witness, in looking at the book, may give evidence which he derives from the book whose accuracy and reliability are unknown factors rather than giving either evidence of his own knowledge or that his information comes form someone upon whom you can assert he relies and considers to be an accurate reporter of events. That's the first problem that I have with this exercise. The second problem, in my submission, is this: I suspect that the list of names comes from "the armed conflict." That, of course, lasts a considerably longer period than the indictment period, and I object to information being given in evidence which falls outside the indictment period or cannot be shown to fall within it, and in effect, I'm objecting to the relevance and probative value of that evidence unless it can be clearly demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, if I may respond. As indicated at paragraph 50, that is book that is -- I propose to show to the witness which has -- he has marked and with green tabs. We also have copies of the members of his family with which he is personally familiar did not survive the conflict. In other words, this is in the opstina Prijedor, that there are some 34 members of his family, and when you look at the document for each of the tabs, there is a photograph of the individual and a date -- a date when they either died or went missing or were exhumed, but the witness' personal knowledge, of course, is when the last time this person has been seen. Now, it's a matter of weight and not admissibility, we would submit, in terms of what the witness can say about this information. He knows that these are members of his extended family. He knows when they disappeared. This book simply provides the photographs and the details of the person, but he can certainly be cross-examined about how he knows whether these people died during the period of indictment or not. That, with the greatest of respect, is not the issue. It just shows that for the wider -- for the wider concern that we have about what happened to the people in Prijedor, we have one family represented that he can actually put names to and tell us what happened to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say the book identifies the date of their disappearance or when they were last seen?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does, and I've showed it to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we will be able to determine whether it falls within the indictment period or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's my understanding. And what we have done is made photocopies of the actual pages, to reduce it down, which have individuals picked out by this witness that are members of his extended family. We have copies for everybody of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can address the court on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'd like to reply, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let him reply and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic first and then Mr. Greaves to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, point number one. We have not received the copies of this book ahead of time so we could meaningful object to the authenticity and the relevance of this matter, but on this point I do concur with Mr. Greaves. Now, two, if this book -- and we have not heard who is the order, how was it prepared, with what degree of accuracy, and I think it would be a lot more appropriate -- it seems to me what the learned counsel of the Prosecution table is going to jog the witness' memory without first exploring the witness' memory to begin with. If he wishes to do so, he might be allowed, but only after witness testifies whether he knows or not and under what circumstances and when certain individuals of his family perished. And I do -- because this is done concurrently and the witness is hearing what we're saying and I do apologise this is a very difficult time for him, but this is our job. Mr. Witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, yes, in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the death or disappearance of someone falls outside the indictment period, it cannot be relevant and cannot be probative. It simply cannot be if it falls outside the indictment period. In my submission, my learned friend is wrong when he asserts it's simply a matter of weight. It cannot be relevant. It cannot be probative of any fact in issue between any of the parties on the indictment if it's outside the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's within the indictment period, then it is relevant and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is potentially relevant and potentially probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we had a list with the relevant dates, much of the force of your objection would fall away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit the book and we'll exclude from our consideration those deaths or disappearances that fall outside the date of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I note the time. Do you wish me to do this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think we must finish, and I have two questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you show this book, please, to the witness? And we have copies for - they are all the same - for their lordships and for my learned friends. I might say, Your Honour, that the witness brought this book with him and has been asked to place green stickers on his family relatives. We have then photocopied those pages and have outlined in yellow on the copies you've now been given the individuals that are his family members that he's referred to on those pages. So you have the yellow highlights as being ones that he's marked on the original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, looking at the book, did you place those green stickers on the individuals of your family who you have indicated are members of your family?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can first of all go -- I'm just going to take the first page, which is marked as page 23. Would you turn to page 23, please, or look at the ELMO there? It would be your first green sticker, in spot number 149 in the book. Do you see that person?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
